$comment: Worked examples executed against the real engine by scripts/run-worked-examples.mjs. Every number published in the documentation comes from running these, never from reading the tables by eye. The 'expect' blocks are regression assertions: a failure on re-run means the engine's behaviour moved and the prose needs rewriting before republishing. Set 'expectThrow': true when the rejection IS the documented behaviour, so the runner reports it without failing. Add scenarios freely — the runner dispatches on any function exported from the engine's index.js.

sections.title: Baseline — no risk multipliers apply
sections.intro: Habitat already on site is scored on what it is and what state it is in. Nothing about the future is being predicted, so neither time nor difficulty enters the sum.

examples.name: 1 ha modified grassland, moderate condition
1 ha coastal saltmarsh, good condition
args: Coastal saltmarsh - Saltmarshes and saline reedbeds

sections.title: The effect of delay and advance on a created habitat
sections.intro: One habitat, one target condition, one hectare — only the timing changes. Creating coastal saltmarsh in good condition normally takes 15 years to reach the target, and reaching merely poor condition takes 1 year. Watch both multipliers move as years are added or removed. Note the jump between 7 and 8 years of advance, and that advance and delay do not simply cancel.

examples.name: Created as planned (no delay, no advance)
args: Coastal saltmarsh - Saltmarshes and saline reedbeds

examples.name: Delayed by 5 years — takes longer to deliver, so the time discount deepens
args: Coastal saltmarsh - Saltmarshes and saline reedbeds

examples.name: Delayed by 20 years — 35 years is past the 30-year ceiling, so it is capped there
args: Coastal saltmarsh - Saltmarshes and saline reedbeds

examples.name: Advanced by 1 year — enough to have reached poor condition already, so the easier enhancement difficulty band is used
args: Coastal saltmarsh - Saltmarshes and saline reedbeds

examples.name: Advanced by 7 years — 8 years of growing still to go, so difficulty still applies
args: Coastal saltmarsh - Saltmarshes and saline reedbeds

examples.name: Advanced by 8 years — head start now exceeds the 7 years remaining, so difficulty drops away entirely
args: Coastal saltmarsh - Saltmarshes and saline reedbeds

examples.name: Advanced by 15 years — fully mature at the point of assessment, so no risk discount at all
args: Coastal saltmarsh - Saltmarshes and saline reedbeds

examples.name: Advanced 5 and delayed 5 — the time multiplier cancels back to the as-planned value, but difficulty does not
args: Coastal saltmarsh - Saltmarshes and saline reedbeds

sections.title: Difficulty depends on the habitat, not just the timing
sections.intro: Same one hectare, same target condition, same timing — different habitats. Harder-to-create habitats keep less of their headline value.

examples.name: Modified grassland (low difficulty to create)
Hazel scrub (medium difficulty to create)
Lowland calcareous grassland (high difficulty to create)

sections.title: The engine reports which difficulty band it chose
sections.intro: Enhancement results name the difficulty band in words alongside the number, so a screen or report can show the reasoning rather than a bare multiplier. The label and the multiplier always agree: low difficulty keeps all of the uplift, medium keeps about two thirds, high keeps about a third. Units are deliberately not shown here — they also depend on distinctiveness, condition and timing, so comparing them across these three rows would not isolate the effect of difficulty.

examples.name: Modified grassland, moderate to good — an easy habitat to improve
Coastal saltmarsh, poor to good — harder
args: Coastal saltmarsh - Saltmarshes and saline reedbeds
Coastal saltmarsh - Saltmarshes and saline reedbeds

examples.name: Lowland calcareous grassland, poor to good — hardest of the three

sections.title: "Standard time to target" is not the number that drives the multiplier
sections.intro: Enhancement results also report the standard time to target — the years the statutory table gives for that habitat and condition change. It is the starting point of the calculation, not its result: advance and delay are applied afterwards. Below, the same improvement is delayed and then advanced. The standard time to target never moves; the time multiplier moves a long way.

examples.name: As planned
Delayed by 10 years — 20 years of waiting in practice
Advanced by 10 years — no waiting at all

sections.title: Retained and enhanced habitat
sections.intro: Retained habitat carries no risk multipliers. Enhancement applies the risk multipliers only to the uplift — the value the habitat already had is never discounted.

examples.name: Retained — 1 ha modified grassland left as it is
Enhanced — 1 ha modified grassland improved from moderate to good
Enhanced, delayed by 10 years — the uplift is discounted harder, the existing value is not

sections.title: Combinations the engine refuses
sections.intro: Not every habitat can be in every condition. Where the statutory tables mark a pairing as not possible, the engine rejects it outright rather than quietly scoring it as zero.

examples.name: A condition the habitat cannot be assessed in
args: Coastal saltmarsh - Saltmarshes and saline reedbeds

examples.name: A habitat that is not in the statutory list

sections.title: Hedgerows follow the same shape
sections.intro: Hedgerows and watercourses are measured in kilometres rather than hectares, and use their own lookup tables, but the rule for choosing multipliers is the same one.

examples.name: Baseline — 1 km native hedgerow, moderate condition
Created — 1 km native hedgerow to good condition, as planned
Created — same hedgerow, delayed by 10 years
